title: Before and after
job: Time clauses: while, until, since, already, not yet
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: Two events pinned to each other, not to the clock. poká is WHILE and takes the IMPERFECTIVE on both sides — two stretches running alongside. poká ne is UNTIL and takes the PERFECTIVE — the one event that ends the wait. That aspect pairing is not a new law: it is L2-M10's rule read off a time clause instead of a bare verb, which is why this module can afford to spend its whole budget on the connectors.

THE ne IN poká ne NEGATES NOTHING. Podozhdíte, poká ya ne vernús' is wait UNTIL I come back — not wait while I do not come back. Read as English reads it the sentence means the opposite of what you meant, and a learner who distrusts the ne simply refuses to write it. Treat poká ne as one word with a hole in the middle: the subject and any other words slot in between, as in poká ya ne vernús'.

RUSSIAN HAS NO PERFECT. I have been waiting an hour is Ya zhdu uzhé chas — a plain present plus an adverb, with no have and no been. L3-M7 said this once about pain; here it is the general rule. The tense you want is the tense the action is IN: still going on means present, over means past. Nothing is missing from the Russian, and there is no form to hunt for.

English SINCE is two words in Russian and the split is by what follows it. A POINT in time takes s plus the GENITIVE: s utrá, since this morning. A stretch reaching back from a moment already mentioned takes s tekh por, since then. Both sit with an ordinary present or past — again, no perfect.

Three time adverbs that English builds with different words. uzhé is ALREADY; yeshchyó ne is NOT YET; and uzhé ne is NOT ANY MORE — the same uzhé, with ne, and nothing added. Each pair is one meaning and is learnt whole: reading uzhé ne as already not gives nothing.

Where English costs nothing: poslé tovó kak and péred tem kak stand exactly where after and before stand, at the front of the clause they govern, with the comma L3-M3 already made compulsory. Bare poslé takes the GENITIVE of a noun (poslé obéda) and chérez takes the ACCUSATIVE for time ahead (chérez chas, in an hour).

sentences.display: Poká ya rabótayu, oná chitáyet knígu.
sentences.script: Пока я работаю, она читает книгу.
sentences.cue: While I'm working, she reads a book.
sentences.literal: While I work, she reads book.

words.note: While, of two stretches running side by side. Both clauses stay IMPERFECTIVE: nothing here reaches an end. With ne after it the word means until instead.

sentences.trap: poká is not when. kogdá (L2-M10) puts one event at another's moment; poká holds two stretches open at once, which is why neither verb may be perfective.
sentences.sound: pa-KA — two syllables, stress on the second, and the unstressed first o is a plain ah.

variations.cue: While I'm working, she's asleep.
variations.changed: a different stretch in the second clause — still imperfective

variations.cue: While she's reading, I work.
variations.changed: the two clauses swapped, which changes nothing but the emphasis

mistake.display: Poká ya rabótayu, oná prochitála knígu.
mistake.script: Пока я работаю, она прочитала книгу.
mistake.why: The perfective prochitála closes the book, and poká has no room for a closed event — it is a window, not a moment. Either chitáyet inside poká, or kogdá with the perfective.

sentences.usage: Saying what someone else is doing during the stretch you are busy.
sentences.mnemonic: poká holds the door open; nothing perfective fits through it.

words.note: Until. The ne is part of the connector and negates nothing; the verb after it is PERFECTIVE, because it is the event that ends the waiting.
Perfective future of vernút'sya, to come back. Its past cells are already taught: vernúlsya and vernúlas' are L2-M10's, vernúlis' is L3-M10's.

sentences.trap: Do not drop the ne to make the sentence look sane. Podozhdíte, poká ya vernús' is not the polite version of this — it is a sentence a Russian has to stop and re-read.
sentences.sound: ver-NUS — stress on the u, and the final s' is soft, the tongue flat against the palate.

variations.cue: Wait until the doctor comes.
variations.changed: poká ne standing next to its verb, which is where it usually sits

variations.cue: Wait until I come back.
variations.changed: the ty form of the command — the connector is untouched

mistake.why: Without ne this is poká, while, with a perfective verb it cannot take — a stretch with a finish line in it. The ne is what turns while into until, and it is not optional.

sentences.usage: Leaving someone somewhere and asking them to stay put.
sentences.mnemonic: Russian waits until NOT-yet-back; the ne is the not, and it belongs to the waiting.

sentences.display: Poslé tovó kak on ushyól, ya pozvoníla Ánne.
sentences.script: После того как он ушёл, я позвонила Анне.
sentences.cue: After he left, I rang Anna.
sentences.literal: After that as he left, I rang to-Anna.

words.note: After, in front of a whole clause. Three words that behave as one and never come apart. For a noun rather than a clause, plain poslé plus the genitive does the job.

sentences.trap: The three words are a unit — tovó is not pointing at anything and kak is not how. Translating them one at a time gives after that as, which is not English and not Russian either.
sentences.sound: pas-LYE ta-VO kak — four beats run together, and the middle word is spelt with g but said with v.

variations.display: Poslé tovó kak on ushyól, ya rabótal dólgo.
variations.script: После того как он ушёл, я работал долго.
variations.cue: After he left, I worked for a long time.
variations.changed: an imperfective stretch after the perfective step

variations.display: Poslé tovó kak oná prishlá, my poshlí v kafé.
variations.script: После того как она пришла, мы пошли в кафе.
variations.cue: After she arrived, we went to a café.
variations.changed: two perfective steps, one after the other

mistake.display: Poslé on ushyól, ya pozvoníla Ánne.
mistake.script: После он ушёл, я позвонила Анне.
mistake.why: Bare poslé cannot govern a clause — it wants a noun in the genitive. In front of he left it needs its other two words: poslé tovó kak.

sentences.usage: Ordering two past events when the second depends on the first being over.
sentences.mnemonic: poslé alone takes a thing; poslé tovó kak takes a whole story.

words.note: Before, and where the two subjects are the same it is followed by the INFINITIVE, not a full clause — péred tem kak otvétit', before answering.
The infinitive of the verb L3-M5 taught in the past, otvétil and otvétila; those two cells stay L3-M5's and only the infinitive opens here.

sentences.trap: English before answering has an -ing; Russian has an infinitive. There is no form of otvétit' that behaves like answering, and nothing to build.
sentences.sound: PYE-rit tyem kak — the first word is front-stressed and its final d hardens to a t.

variations.display: Péred tem kak otvétit', ya vsegdá dúmayu.
variations.script: Перед тем как ответить, я всегда думаю.
variations.cue: Before answering, I always think.
variations.changed: a habit in the main clause instead of a command

variations.display: Péred tem kak spat', ya chitáyu knígu.
variations.script: Перед тем как спать, я читаю книгу.
variations.cue: Before going to sleep, I read a book.
variations.changed: a different infinitive in the same slot

mistake.why: Bare péred is a preposition and cannot stand in front of a verb at all. The connector that can is the three-word péred tem kak.

sentences.usage: Advice, instructions, and anything printed above a form.
sentences.mnemonic: Before an ACTION, Russian names the action with its plain infinitive — no -ing to build.

sentences.display: Ya zdes' s utrá, i óchen' ustál.
sentences.script: Я здесь с утра, и очень устал.
sentences.cue: I've been here since this morning, and I'm very tired.
sentences.literal: I here since morning, and very tired.

words.note: The genitive s takes for a point in time: s utrá, since this morning. Note the stress moves off the first syllable — útro but s utrá.

sentences.trap: There is no verb in the Russian at all, and none is missing. I have been here needs a have and a been in English; Russian needs only Ya zdes' plus the point the being started from.
sentences.sound: s oot-RA — the s leans on the next word and the stress lands on the final a.

variations.cue: I've been here since this morning.
variations.changed: the bare frame, with nothing hung on it

variations.display: Oná zdes' s utrá, i óchen' ustála.
variations.script: Она здесь с утра, и очень устала.
variations.cue: She's been here since this morning, and she's very tired.
variations.changed: a woman speaking, so ustál becomes ustála

mistake.display: Ya byl zdes' s utrá, i óchen' ustál.
mistake.script: Я был здесь с утра, и очень устал.
mistake.why: Correct Russian, and it says something else: with byl you have left. The present tense is what keeps you standing there, which is exactly the work English gives to have been.

sentences.usage: Explaining, with some feeling, how long you have already been somewhere.
sentences.mnemonic: Still true, still present tense — Russian marks the start and lets the tense say it is not over.

sentences.cue: I've been waiting for you for an hour.

words.note: Present of zhdat', to wait. It takes its object bare — zhdu vas, no preposition, where English needs for.

sentences.trap: Two English habits to drop at once: the perfect (have been waiting) and the for in waiting FOR you. Russian has neither — a present tense and a bare object.
sentences.sound: zhdoo — one syllable, and the zh is the s of pleasure said hard, straight into the d.

variations.display: Ya zhdu vas uzhé dva chasá.
variations.script: Я жду вас уже два часа.
variations.cue: I've been waiting for you for two hours.
variations.changed: a longer stretch, and the counted form of chas

variations.cue: He's waiting for you here.
variations.changed: the third person of the same verb

mistake.why: The past says the waiting is over and you have gone. If you are still standing there, the tense that says so is the present — uzhé alone carries the whole hour.

sentences.usage: Said with an edge, to someone an hour late.
sentences.mnemonic: Still waiting means still present; uzhé does the work of have been.

sentences.display: Oná yeshchyó ne prishlá, i ya bespokóyus'.
sentences.script: Она ещё не пришла, и я беспокоюсь.
sentences.cue: She hasn't come yet, and I'm worried.
sentences.literal: She still not came, and I worry.

words.note: Not yet, learnt whole. L1-M8's yeshchyó on its own is still or more; with ne in front of a perfective past it says the thing has not happened so far.

sentences.trap: English puts yet at the END of the sentence; Russian puts yeshchyó ne in front of the verb and never at the end. She hasn't come yet is Oná yeshchyó ne prishlá, word for word not-yet came.
sentences.sound: yish-CHO nye — the shch is a long soft sh, and the two words run together as one.

variations.cue: He hasn't come yet.
variations.changed: a man arriving, so prishlá becomes prishyól

variations.cue: She hasn't rung yet.
variations.changed: a different perfective under the same not-yet

mistake.why: Heard, but it reads as an afterthought tacked on. The pair belongs together and in front of the verb; splitting it is what an English speaker does on the first day and stops doing on the second.

sentences.usage: Reporting that someone expected has still not turned up.
sentences.mnemonic: Not-yet is one word in Russian's head: yeshchyó ne, glued, and always before the verb.

sentences.display: Ya uzhé ne zhivú v Moskvé.
sentences.script: Я уже не живу в Москве.
sentences.cue: I don't live in Moscow any more.
sentences.literal: I already not live in Moscow.

words.note: Not any more. Two words the learner already owns — L2-M5's uzhé and L1-M3's ne — meaning something neither of them means alone. Take it whole.

sentences.trap: already not is a dead end. uzhé ne is not any more, and English builds that idea out of a third word (more) that has no counterpart here at all.
sentences.sound: oo-ZHE nye — stress on the second syllable of uzhé, and the zh is soft-edged but not palatal.

variations.cue: I don't work there any more.
variations.changed: a different thing that has stopped being true

variations.cue: He doesn't live here any more.
variations.changed: the third person, and here instead of Moscow

mistake.display: Ya ne zhivú v Moskvé ból'she.
mistake.script: Я не живу в Москве больше.
mistake.why: Built out of L2-M9's ból'she, more, the way English builds it — and it lands as a heavier, arguing sentence. The plain way to say it is uzhé ne in front of the verb.

sentences.usage: Correcting an assumption someone still holds about you.
sentences.mnemonic: uzhé ne: already-not, which is Russian for not any longer.

sentences.display: S tekh por on ne zvoníl.
sentences.script: С тех пор он не звонил.
sentences.literal: Since those times he not rang.

words.note: Since then — three words taken whole, pointing back at a moment already mentioned. For a named point in time use s plus the genitive instead: s utrá.

sentences.trap: English since covers both jobs; Russian splits them. s utrá needs a noun in the genitive; s tekh por needs no noun at all, because the moment is one you have already given.
sentences.sound: s tyekh POR — three short words, the stress at the end, and the s glued to the front.

variations.display: S tekh por oná ne rabótayet.
variations.script: С тех пор она не работает.
variations.cue: She hasn't worked since then.
variations.changed: a present tense — the state is still running

variations.display: S tekh por my ne býli tam.
variations.script: С тех пор мы не были там.
variations.cue: We haven't been there since then.
variations.changed: a past that has simply not happened again

mistake.display: S tot vrémeni on ne zvoníl.
mistake.script: С тот времени он не звонил.
mistake.why: An attempt to build since that time out of parts. The phrase Russian actually uses is frozen — s tekh por — and nothing about it is assembled fresh.

sentences.usage: Closing off a stretch that began with something you have just described.
sentences.mnemonic: s tekh por: from those times — a fixed three-word since-then that never changes shape.

sentences.display: Ya pozvonyú vam poslé obéda, chérez dva chasá.
sentences.script: Я позвоню вам после обеда, через два часа.
sentences.cue: I'll ring you after lunch, in two hours' time.
sentences.literal: I will-ring to-you after lunch, through two hours.

words.note: After, in front of a noun in the GENITIVE. L2-M10 taught the phrase poslé étovo whole; the bare preposition, free to take any noun, opens here.
Lunch, the midday meal. The -a is the genitive poslé demands; the dictionary form is obéd.
Time ahead, measured from now, with the ACCUSATIVE: chérez chas, in an hour. English says in; poslé would say after some other event, which is a different claim.

sentences.trap: English uses in for both in an hour and in the morning. Russian splits them: chérez chas is a stretch counted forward from now, and v is what puts you inside a time.
sentences.sound: CHE-riz — front-stressed, and the final z softens towards the word after it.

variations.cue: I'll ring you after work.
variations.changed: another noun in the genitive after poslé

variations.cue: I'll be back in an hour.
variations.changed: chérez on its own, with no after-clause beside it

mistake.display: Ya pozvonyú vam v dva chasá.
mistake.script: Я позвоню вам в два часа.
mistake.why: Correct Russian saying something else: v dva chasá is at two o'clock, a point on the clock. chérez dva chasá is two hours from now, whatever the clock says.

sentences.usage: Promising a call and pinning it to both an event and a stretch.
sentences.mnemonic: poslé looks back at an event; chérez counts forward from this minute.

comprehensionPool.display: Poká ya rabótayu, oná chitáyet gazétu.
comprehensionPool.script: Пока я работаю, она читает газету.
comprehensionPool.cue: While I'm working, she reads the paper.

comprehensionPool.display: Poslé tovó kak on ushyól, my poshlí domóy.
comprehensionPool.script: После того как он ушёл, мы пошли домой.
comprehensionPool.cue: After he left, we went home.
I've been here since this morning.
I've been waiting for you for an hour.

comprehensionPool.display: Ya uzhé ne zhivú v Moskvé.
comprehensionPool.script: Я уже не живу в Москве.
comprehensionPool.cue: I don't live in Moscow any more.

comprehensionPool.display: S tekh por on ne zvoníl.
comprehensionPool.script: С тех пор он не звонил.

comprehensionPool.cue: I'll ring you in an hour.

comprehensionPool.display: Poká ne pridyót vrach, ya búdu zdes'.
comprehensionPool.script: Пока не придёт врач, я буду здесь.
comprehensionPool.cue: I'll be here until the doctor comes.
He's waiting for you after lunch.
